cards.explanation: The answer is True. The LORD’s words name “…oxen and sheep, camels and donkeys.” The animals are in the command right alongside the people. It's a heavy command, and the story doesn't hurry past it. Keep those animals in mind, friends, because they come back.

The answer is that the Kenites were kind to Israel leaving Egypt. Saul tells the Kenites, “Since you showed kindness to all the Israelites when they came up out of Egypt, go on and get away from the Amalekites.” That kindness got them a warning and a way out. It's a good reminder, friends, that a kind thing you did can still be remembered later.

The answer is False. The Kenites listen. Verse 6 ends with “So the Kenites moved away from the Amalekites.” Saul warned them, and they moved away. Me, I've ignored a warning or two in my day, mostly about the oven.
The answer is Agag, friends. The text says Saul “…captured Agag king of Amalek alive…” Hang on to that name. A king captured alive is a detail you don't want to lose track of.

The answer is best, friends. Saul and his troops spared “…the best of the sheep and cattle, the fat calves and lambs, and the best of everything else.” Verse 9 puts it plainly. Best is the word to remember.

The answer is whatever was despised and worthless. The text says “…they devoted to destruction all that was despised and worthless.” In this verse, the best is what they were unwilling to devote. So Saul and his troops spared the best and devoted what was despised and worthless.

The answer is regrets. The LORD says, “I regret that I have made Saul king, for he has turned away from following Me and has not carried out My instructions.” That's a hard line to read, friends. The LORD gives the reason right there in the verse.

The answer is that Samuel cries out to the LORD all night. Samuel was distressed, and he “…cried out to the LORD all that night.” The text puts his night with the LORD. I think that tells you how much it hit him.

The answer is a monument for himself, friends. Samuel is told that Saul “…has set up a monument for himself and has turned and gone down to Gilgal.” Samuel hears it secondhand, from whoever told him. Me, I've got my name carved on my handle by the Millers, and I'd never ask for a monument on top of it.
The answer is True. Saul says, “May the LORD bless you. I have carried out the LORD’s instructions.” He says it in the same breath as the greeting. Samuel hasn't asked a single question yet.

The answer is sheep bleating and cattle lowing, friends. Samuel asks, “Then what is this bleating of sheep and lowing of cattle that I hear?” Saul had just said the job was done, and the animals didn't get the memo. Sheep are terrible at keeping secrets.
The answer is the troops, friends. Saul answers, “The troops brought them from the Amalekites…” When one of my batches burns, I blame the oven. Saul reaches for the troops.
The answer is to sacrifice to the LORD. Saul says they spared the best sheep and cattle “…to sacrifice to the LORD your God…” It sounds holy, friends. But Samuel isn't done talking yet.

The answer is plunder, friends. Samuel asks, “So why did you not obey the LORD? Why did you rush upon the plunder and do evil in the sight of the LORD?” Plunder is what's taken from a defeated enemy. Rush upon is a strong phrase, and Samuel chose it.

The answer is False, friends. Saul answers Samuel with “But I did obey the LORD…” and he says he went on the mission and brought back Agag king of Amalek. No admission yet. That comes later in the chapter.

The answer is obeying the LORD's voice. Samuel says, “Behold, obedience is better than sacrifice, and attentiveness is better than the fat of rams.” Saul kept pointing at sacrifices, and Samuel points at listening. Obeying the LORD's voice is what he says is better.

The answer is that the LORD rejected Saul as king, friends. Samuel says, “Because you have rejected the word of the LORD, He has rejected you as king.” That's a big line. Saul pushed aside the word of the LORD, and Samuel tells him where it leaves him.

The answer is that he feared the people and obeyed them, friends. Saul says, “I have sinned; I have transgressed the LORD’s commandment and your instructions, because I feared the people and obeyed their voice.” He says it plainly. That's a real thing to say out loud.

The answer is that Saul asks Samuel to forgive him and come back with him. Saul says, “Now therefore, please forgive my sin and return with me so I can worship the LORD.” He asks for forgiveness and for company. I think it's a lot to put in one sentence.

The answer is False, friends. Samuel answers, “I will not return with you. For you have rejected the word of the LORD, and He has rejected you as king over Israel.” That first answer is a no. It's a hard moment, and Samuel doesn't soften it.
The answer is tears. Saul grabbed the hem of Samuel's robe, “…and it tore.” One grab, one rip. And Samuel is about to say something about it.

The answer is the kingdom, friends. Samuel says, “The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today…” Right before this, Saul grabbed the hem of Samuel's robe, and it tore (1 Samuel 15:27). A robe tears, and then Samuel speaks of a kingdom torn.
The answer is neighbor, friends. Samuel says the LORD “…has given it to your neighbor who is better than you.” He doesn't name him here. I'd say that's a mystery worth keeping.
The answer is honor, friends. Saul says, “Please honor me now before the elders of my people and before Israel.” He wants it done in front of them. I think that stands out after what he just heard.
The answer is True, friends. The text says, “So Samuel went back with Saul, and Saul worshiped the LORD.” The first time Samuel said no. This time Samuel goes back with him.
The answer is that Agag thinks the danger of death is behind him. The text says, “Surely the bitterness of death is past.” He walks up cheerfully, friends, and he's sure of it. This part is heavy.
The answer is Gibeah, friends. The text says Samuel went to Ramah, “…but Saul went up to his home in Gibeah of Saul.” They go separate ways after this. Gibeah is the home the text names for Saul.

The answer is False, friends. The text says, “And to the day of his death, Samuel never again visited Saul. Samuel mourned for Saul…” So Samuel did not visit him again. I think that's a sad ending to this part of the story.
